paragraphs: The Argentine lomito completo turns a thin beef tenderloin or sirloin cutlet into a substantial sandwich with ham, melted cheese, lettuce, tomato, mayonnaise, and a fried egg.

The lomito is found across Argentina and neighboring countries, with regional disagreement over the “complete” toppings. This version follows the Argentine fast-food pattern of thin beef, ham, cheese, egg, lettuce, tomato, and mayonnaise. This Kwilt version follows the reviewed household adaptation: Use the recognizably Argentine completo architecture while omitting redundant ketchup and mustard so beef, egg, and melted cheese remain legible.

paragraphs: Lima's butifarra sandwich centers jamón del país—thin slices of red-spiced pork—inside pan francés with lettuce and sharp, herb-flecked salsa criolla.

Peruvian butifarra is a Lima sanguchería sandwich, unrelated in form to Catalan botifarra sausage. Its defining meat is jamón del país: cooked pork colored and flavored with garlic, achiote, cumin, oregano, and Peruvian chile. This Kwilt version follows the reviewed household adaptation: Author an oven-braised home jamón del país with transparent pan-francés substitution, keeping mayonnaise optional and letting salsa criolla provide the moisture.

origin.label: Bauru, São Paulo
origin.region: São Paulo café and sandwich cooking

paragraphs: The original Bauru was created at São Paulo's Ponto Chic and is defined by a hollowed crisp roll, thin roast beef, tomato and pickles, and a molten blend of cheeses rather than the later ham-and-cheese shorthand.

The Bauru was created at Ponto Chic in São Paulo for Casimiro Pinto Neto, nicknamed Bauru. The protected original is roast beef, melted cheese, tomato, and cucumber pickle in pão francês; the common ham-cheese-tomato “Bauru” is a later namesake. This Kwilt version follows the reviewed household adaptation: Reproduce the documented original with a practical four-cheese blend and scratch roast beef, resisting the widespread ham-and-cheese reinterpretation.
